text.p: A British election is due within two months and speculation is mounting day by day about when Prime Minister John Major will call it.
The latest this election can legally be held is May 22 but Major has said he would not call it later than May 1. That is thought to be his preferred date and is only seven weeks away.
If Major calls a May 1 poll, he must dissolve parliament at least 17 working days beforehand -- April 8 or earlier.
But it is usual for the prime minister to give several days' notice of the dissolution of parliament.
Former premier Margaret Thatcher gave four and seven days' warning in 1983 and 1987, respectively, while Major provided five days' notice at the 1992 election.
So a May 1 poll would probably be called around the start of April. An Easter holiday break means that Friday, March 28 and Monday, March 31 are non-working days.
So Major could make an announcement either straight after Easter or just before. These are the dates members of parliament in Westminster see now as most likely.

But the government is not duty-bound to call an election as late as possible. Some political commentators think it will launch a longer campaign to allow more time to slice away at Labour's lead of 20 points and more in the opinion polls.
Conservative strategists believe the longer Major leaves it, the more opportunities there are for Labour leader Tony Blair, untested by office, to slip up and start to lose his lead.
As a result, the announcement could come at any time -- hence all the speculation and the massed ranks of photographers loitering outside 10 Downing St, Major's official residence.
The chance to call an April 10 election, another favoured date, came and went on Wednesday. An April 17 vote would have to be called next week.
Traditionally, British elections are held on Thursdays.
But whenever the day is named, Major made it clear on Thursday that it will not happen this week.
"There will be no announcement at or before Bath. I am not going to speculate beyond that," he said in an interview with the Western Daily Press newspaper.
The ruling Conservative party's semi-annual conference takes place this Friday and Saturday in the western England city of Bath. Major will speak on the second day.
